title: Panoptik
pitch: Panoptik is a browser-native video studio powered by WebMCP. In-browser AI agents inspect footage and propose smart cuts and zooms as reviewable staged diffs—100% locally.
about_excerpt: Panoptik is a browser-native video studio powered by WebMCP. In-browser AI agents inspect footage and propose smart cuts and zooms as reviewable staged diffs—100% locally. Like 1 Comment Story Updates WebMCP Toolcalls - 2 Zoom controls Voiceover and music Zoom points Stage WebMCP Toolcalls - 1 Text overlays Landing page Facecam controls Autogenerated captions using whisper agentic ediditing session Export menu Workspace Editor Panoptik × WebMCP — Project Story A browser-native video studio where humans and AI agents co-edit on the same canvas. > Decode, render, audio mixing, and export happen 100% inside your browser using WebCodecs and Canvas2D. No uploads, no render farm, zero data leakage. Inspiration Making demo videos for software products takes too much time. A punchy 90-second product demo requires 15+ camera zoom keyframes, dozens of subtitle snippets, manual silence excision, and canvas framing. In tools like ScreenStudio, Loom, or Premiere, this forces creators to spend 45 to 60 minutes scrubbing frame-by-frame, calculating focal centers, placing timeline diamonds, and proofreading speech. Because editing is so exhausting, many developers simply give up and ship raw, unpolished recordings. When we set out to build an AI agent to handle this tedious workflow, we ran into a core architectural barrier: video editing lives inside client-side canvas pixels. Backend MCP servers are blind to the browser session: The video file lives in the browser's Origin Private File System (OPFS), the playback state lives in an in-memory Zustand store, and the rendered UI exists only as Canvas2D pixel buffers. There is no remote server copy for an external API to inspect. Multimodal DOM-scraping is fragile and costly: Directing an agent via automated screenshots and synthetic cursor events consumes ~150 KB to 200 KB of token bandwidth per action, introduces seconds of latency, and frequently misclicks or desynchronizes with the timeline. The OpenAI WebMCP Challenge provided the missing architectural link: an in-page, standardized communication bridge between browser-resident agents and client-side web applications. We built Panoptik so an in-browser agent can inspect the canvas, analyze project telemetry, and propose structured edits directly through 30 imperative WebMCP tools—while keeping the human firmly in control. What it does Panoptik is a screen recording and video production studio that runs entirely inside the browser: Zero-Upload Local Media Engine: Drop in raw recordings or capture screen, camera, and microphone directly. Decoding, real-time compositing, audio mixing, and MP4/WebM encoding run entirely client-side via WebCodecs, Canvas2D, and mediabunny. Proprietary dashboards, sensitive credentials, and internal code never leave your machine. 30 Granular WebMCP Tools: Panoptik exposes its editing engine via document.modelContext.registerTool() . Running inside ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled, the agent inspects scene cadence, reads click coordinates, checks rendered frames, and orchestrates multi-track edits. The "Agent Proposes, Human Disposes" Diff Engine: The agent never silently mutates the timeline. Proposed cuts, zooms, captions, and transitions appear as non-destructive ghost edits (dashed amber keyframe diamonds, pending caption chips, and preview diffs). The creator can adjust any parameter manually and commit or discard the diff with a single click. Studio-Grade Polish: Dynamic Camera Zooms: Smooth continuous cubic camera translations with automatic viewport margin clamping. Visual Grounding: Three-tier focal resolution mapping agent requests (e.g., "zoom in on the login button" ) to exact coordinates via click telemetry, grid bounding boxes, or balanced fallbacks. Acoustic Snapping & Silence Removal: Automatic dead-air truncation that preserves natural speech cadence without clipping vocal phonemes. Word-Level Subtitles: Synchronized transcription with animated keyword highlighting. Pitch-Preserving Speed Adjustment: High-fidelity audio time-stretching via the WSOLA algorithm. Live Tool Trace Panel: A persistent inspector panel that surfaces every WebMCP call, runtime latency, input payload, and return value for total human oversight. How we built it Panoptik is structured as a monorepo containing the Next.js application ( apps/web ), the low-level media engine ( packages/engine ), and the shared type contract ( packages/project-schema ). ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Browser Tab (Next.js) │ │ │ │ ┌──────────────┐ ┌────────────────┐ ┌─────────────┐ │ │ │Preview Canvas│ │Timeline & Store│ │ Tool Trace │ │ │ └──────┬───────┘ └───────┬────────┘ └─────────────┘ │ │ │ │ │ │ ▼ ▼ │ │ ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ │ │ Reactive Project Store (Zustand) │ │ │ │ Committed Elements ↔ Staged Ghost Diffs │ │ │ └──────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────┘ │ │ │ │ │ ┌───────────────────┴───────────────────┐ │ │ ▼ ▼ │ │ ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ │ │ │Media Engine │ │ WebMCP Layer │ │ │ │(WebCodecs, │ │ (30 Tools, │ │ │ │ Canvas2D) │ │ Snapping) │ │ │ └──────┬───────┘ └──────┬───────┘ │ │ │ │ │ │ ▼ ▼ │ │ ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ │ │ W3C document.modelContext / Web APIs │ │ │ │ VideoDecoder · VideoEncoder · OPFS · Mediabunny │ │ │ └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │ └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ 1. Camera Zoom Interpolation At any playback timestamp t , the camera transform state is represented by a 2D affine vector: T(t) = [ s(t), x_f(t), y_f(t) ]ᵀ where s(t) is the zoom scale factor and (x_f, y_f) ∈ [0, 1]² is the normalized focal target. For a zoom starting at t_k with duration Δt , the normalized transition progress parameter is: p(t) = clamp( (t - t_k) / Δt, 0, 1 ) Progress is mapped through a cubic easing curve E(p) : E(p) = 4p³ (for p < 0.5) E(p) = 1 - (-2p + 2)³ / 2 (for p ≥ 0.5) The camera blends smoothly from the current state to the target state: T(t) = (1 - E(p)) · T_start + E(p) · T_target To render this on a canvas of dimensions (W_canvas, H_canvas) letterboxing a source video (W_vid, H_vid) with base scale S_0 , the 2D transformation offsets applied to the context are: T_x(t) = (W_canvas / 2) - x_f(t) · W_vid · S_0 · s(t) T_y(t) = (H_canvas / 2) - y_f(t) · H_vid · S_0 · s(t) 2. Dual Time-Space Mapping The human editor and agent reason in timeline time ( t_timeline ), while underlying video chunks exist in immutable source time ( t_src ). Cuts and speed modifications cause these coordinate systems to diverge. For clip i with source interval [s_i, e_i] played at speed factor v_i , the timeline duration is: D_i = (e_i - s_i) / v_i The forward mapping function transforms source seconds into timeline seconds: t_timeline = ∑(D_j) + (t_src - s_k) / v_k When an agent proposes an edit, Panoptik immediately maps the timestamp back into source coordinates using the inverse mapping. Downstream timeline shifts caused by cutting dead air never invalidate or displace previously anchored keyframes. 3. Acoustic Word Boundary Snapping Rather than blindly executing raw timestamps emitted by an LLM, cut proposals are guarded against active vocal phonemes using an acoustic safety boundary: |t_cut - t_boundary(w)| ≥ 150 ms (for all spoken words w) If a proposed cut falls within 150 ms of a word boundary, the cut automatically snaps outward to the nearest preceding silence interval, preventing clipped syllables. 4. Token & Bandwidth Economics Comparing WebMCP structured tool calls against conventional multimodal vision scraping: WebMCP Payload: ~2.1 KB Screenshot + DOM Scraping: ~165 KB Efficiency Gain: 1 - (2.1 KB / 165 KB) ≈ 98.7% A complete multi-step edit session completes in ~6 lightweight JSON tool calls (~3 KB total context overhead), eliminating latency bottlenecks and model context exhaustion. Challenges we ran into Zero-WASM, Pure Browser Media Pipeline: Most web video editors rely on ffmpeg.wasm , which requires massive binary downloads (30 MB+), induces heavy CPU thermal throttling, and risks memory leaks. We built on native web standards: WebCodecs VideoDecoder / VideoEncoder , Canvas2D, and OPFS. Handling variable frame rate (VFR) screen recordings while maintaining microsecond audio synchronization required custom timestamp interpolation and frame-stepping logic. The "Dual Time-Space Paradox" in Agent Reasoning: LLMs reason sequentially based on current visuals: "cut dead air from 0:12 to 0:18, then zoom in at 0:25" . As soon as the first cut is staged, the visual timeline contracts by 6 seconds. If the subsequent zoom is evaluated against the old timeline, it lands on the wrong frame. We solved this by implementing an atomic batch execution pipeline ( propose_edits ) that evaluates all instructions against a single snapshot and performs dynamic cut-map rebasing.
